label: rem:strong-multiplicativity-poisson-lie
title: Strong multiplicativity, primitives and Poisson–Lie groups
html:
This remark records four facts about strong multiplicativity: what it says on primitive elements, where the \pi \otimes \pi term matters, how it relates to Poisson–Lie groups, and how it relates to Proposition 1.13 of [leitner2006].

Primitive elements. Suppose x, y \in T are primitive, \Delta x = x \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes x and likewise for y. Applying 1 \otimes \tau \otimes 1 to \Delta x \otimes \Delta y gives four terms, which pair the tensor factors as (x, y)(1, 1), (x, 1)(1, y), (1, y)(x, 1) and (1, 1)(x, y). A Poisson structure is a biderivation, so \pi(a, 1) = \pi(1, a) = 0. Every term therefore kills \pi \otimes \pi, and only the first and last survive, giving

\Delta\,\pi(x, y) \;=\; \pi(x, y) \otimes 1 \;+\; 1 \otimes \pi(x, y).

So at a pair of primitive elements, strong multiplicativity says exactly that \pi(x, y) is primitive. This is proved in Lean as Fred2005.StrongMult.strongMult_prim_iff, for any bracket with \pi(a, 1) = \pi(1, a) = 0 on a not necessarily commutative algebra. For the tensor algebra of a Lie algebra \mathfrak{g} with \Delta induced by the diagonal of \mathfrak{g}, the elements of \mathfrak{g} are primitive, and [leitner2006], Remark 1.12.2, notes that the \pi \otimes \pi term vanishes there.

Non-primitive elements. The \pi \otimes \pi term matters on non-primitive basis elements. For example \Delta(x^2) contains 2\,x \otimes x, so the right-hand side for \pi(x^2, z^2) contains 4\,\pi(x, z) \otimes \pi(x, z). In characteristic p the coordinate algebras A_i carry divided powers, and the condition has content there.

Poisson–Lie groups. Without the \pi \otimes \pi term the condition reads \Delta \circ \pi = (\cdot \otimes \pi + \pi \otimes \cdot) \circ (1 \otimes \tau \otimes 1) \circ \Delta. The operator on the right is the product Poisson bracket on S \otimes S, \{a \otimes b, c \otimes d\} = ac \otimes \{b, d\} + \{a, c\} \otimes bd. So the truncated condition says \Delta is a map of Poisson algebras. For a group G with coordinate algebra S, that is the statement that multiplication G \times G \to G is a Poisson map, which is the multiplicativity of a Poisson–Lie group [luweinstein1990]. Strong multiplicativity adds the quadratic term \pi \otimes \pi, which records the deformation of the product of S to that of U.

Relation to Proposition 1.13. Proposition 1.13 of [leitner2006] proves one direction: if \Delta is strongly multiplicative, it vanishes on the relations g_{y,x} = yx - xy - \pi(y, x), so it descends to an algebra map U \to U \otimes U. Remark 1.12.2 of the same paper says that, for a Lie algebra, the condition can be viewed as exactly what is needed for \Delta to descend. A proof of the converse would have to work in U \otimes U rather than in T \otimes T, using the normal forms of Theorem 1.9. It is not given there or here.
